newsitem.title: USA: New age economics leaves some experts baffled.
newsitem.headline: New age economics leaves some experts baffled.

text.p: These are trying times for economists. The U.S. economy is performing amazingly well, but even the world's most important central banker, Alan Greenspan, cannot explain what is going on.

"Many observers, including us, have been puzzled ... It will, doubtless, be several years before we know with any conviction the full story of the surprisingly benign combination of output and prices," he said in his half-yearly Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress last week.

Greenspan is not the only one who appears at a loss. "I believe that the recent performance of the economy is to some degree a puzzle," agreed Federal Reserve Board member Laurence Meyer in separate testimony to a House committee.
The old jokes are proving partly true -- if you ask 10 economists what is going on, you will get 10 answers.
But whatever the right answer may be, it works for the average American. The economic picture at United States Inc. is almost too good to be true.

Unemployment is at a mere 5 percent, consumer prices rose at a mere 1.4 percent annual pace in the first half of 1997 -- an 11-year low -- and output rose at an annualized 5.9 percent clip in the first quarter, well above the rate that most economists would traditionally characterise as sustainable in the long run.
Is this the new age of economics? Has the traditional Phillips model, which claims there is a long-run tradeoff between unemployment and inflation, failed?
Well -- yes and no, analysts say. Most economists advise against consigning those well-thumbed macroeconomics textbooks to the scrapheap.

At least some of the recent stellar performance of the U.S. economy seems to be attributable to structural changes, such as increased productivity. Most observers agree that a range of temporary factors -- so-called positive supply shocks -- also play a big role in the final equation.
"I've seen this before. We're having luck and some good management," David Wyss, of Massachusetts-based DRI/McGraw Hill, told Reuters. "It's primarily temporary."

Experts cite the strong dollar, which helps to keep import prices down, and low oil prices as among the key reasons for the recent lull in inflation. Higher labour mobility, more moderate wage agreements and a drastic fall in health care costs also had a strong impact, they say.
"There is no evidence that there is a major shift in economic performance, no evidence of a major structural change," said Wyss.
Other economists, however, are not quite as convinced.

"This economic success isn't a result of only temporary factors or luck, but rather derives in large part from good economic policy choices and from favourable structural shifts," said John Lipsky, chief economist at Chase Manhattan, in his own testimony to the House Banking committee this week.
He said today's workers produce more in less time, primarily because the large-scale use of computers is helping them to do a better job.

Gordon Richards, an economist at the National Association of Manufacturers, took a similar line when he addressed lawmakers. "As a result of structural changes during the 1990s, the economy can now achieve faster growth with continued low inflation," he said.

Greenspan himself said that while recent performance has been "exceptional," the economy was undergoing some "basic improvements" based on technological progress that allowed productivity to rise, thereby boosting corporate earnings.

Financial markets heard what they wanted to hear, and investors promptly pushed up the Dow Jones industrial average to a record close of 8,116.93 points on Thursday, before the index eased slightly on Friday to close the week at 8,113.44.

But few insiders appear ready to surrender fully to the boundless optimism. Both analysts and Fed officials are now sitting tight, watching for the first signs that the old models may, after all, not be as dead as some seem to believe.

"I have no doubt that the current stance of policy will need to be changed at some point," Greenspan said. "The Federal Reserve must be alert to the possibility that additional action might be called for to forestall excessive credit creation."
